title: The skull on the water (Avot 2:6)
hookLine: Hillel sees a skull floating and says: because you drowned others, you were drowned

cards: Hillel is at the water's edge. Something is floating on the surface, turning slowly in the current. He looks closer.
It's a human skull. He doesn't scream, and he doesn't walk away. He speaks to it: only a handful of words, in Aramaic, the everyday language of his time.
Pirkei Avot is mostly sayings, short, wise, a little abstract. And right in the middle of chapter two sits this scene out of a ghost story.

teach.h: A SKULL, AND A FEW WORDS.
teach.b: Here's what he says. Because you drowned others, they drowned you. And in the end, the ones who drowned you will be drowned.
That's the whole thing. The Mishnah doesn't say whose skull it was, or where, or when, or how Hillel knew. Only the words.
The first half sounds like simple payback: you did it, so it was done to you.
The rabbis have a name for this idea, measure for measure: what a person sends out tends to come back in kind. But the second half is where the saying turns.
The ones who drowned you will be drowned too. The people who killed this man aren't heroes of justice.
They've just joined the cycle, and it doesn't stop with them. Violence answered by violence doesn't end anything; it hands the drowning on to the next person. Commentators are careful here.
This isn't a claim that everyone who suffers must have deserved it. Hillel is speaking to one skull, not about every victim in the world.

Some commentators read it as a statement about God's justice, which works in ways people can't see and don't get to take into their own hands. So it's a warning in two directions. Don't be the one who drowns others.
And don't appoint yourself to drown the drowner.
Harm comes back. The only way out of the circle is for someone to stop pushing.

how: Jewish teaching speaks of 'measure for measure' (middah keneged middah) as a pattern in how the world works, while leaving judgment to God and the courts rather than to private revenge.

o: the sage who spoke to a skull floating on the water
a prophet who warned the kings against revenge
a scribe who copied the Mishnah onto scrolls

games.q: what's inside the scene — tap the pairs.
p: what you send out comes back

s: the Mishnah says whose skull it was
it gives no name, no place, no time. only Hillel's words.
Hillel spoke to the skull in Aramaic
the everyday language of his time, not the Hebrew of most of Avot.
the saying praises the ones who drowned the drowner
they will be drowned too. the cycle doesn't end with them.

games.q: someone makes a cutting remark about you in front of friends. what does Hillel's skull suggest?
o: cut back harder, so they learn.
don't hand the harm back. let the circle stop.
games.why: those who drowned you will be drowned: the ones who answer harm with harm just join the cycle. someone has to stop pushing.

practice: Think of a small circle of hurt going back and forth in your life, nothing dramatic: a sibling who snipes and you snipe back, a coworker you both undercut, a comment section.
Imagine the next turn is yours, and you simply don't take it, no reply in kind. Picture the circle slowing down.

wordCard.voice: Hillel, who spoke to a skull floating on the water: because you drowned others, they drowned you, and so will those who drowned you.

orig.note: Aramaic: because you drowned others, they drowned you.

carryVoice: Your line: harm comes back. Measure for measure, unless someone stops pushing. See you tomorrow.
